reviews.scope: Proving the polygon exterior angle sum is 360 degrees
reviews.reason: The interior angle sum formula supports the algebraic proof via supplementary linear pairs at each vertex, which is one specific derivation method for the exterior angle sum.
reviews.counterexample: One can justify the 360-degree exterior angle sum by translating exterior angle rays to a common vertex or summing total turning angles around the perimeter.

reviews.scope: Defining sides, interior angles, and diagonals of a parallelogram
reviews.reason: Stating and proving that a parallelogram has equal opposite sides, equal opposite angles, and bisecting diagonals requires the foundational concepts of polygon sides, interior angles, and diagonals.

reviews.scope: Proving the side, angle, and diagonal properties of parallelograms
reviews.reason: Deductively proving that opposite sides and angles are equal and that diagonals bisect each other relies on constructing diagonals and writing complete triangle congruence proofs.

reviews.scope: Formulating and proving the criteria for identifying a parallelogram
reviews.reason: Understanding what a parallelogram is and formulating its identification criteria as converses of its side, angle, and diagonal relationships directly build on the parallelogram concept and properties.

reviews.scope: Proving opposite sides are parallel to establish a parallelogram
reviews.reason: Deductively proving the parallelogram criteria and applying parallel-side tests require establishing line parallelism from equal alternate interior angles or supplementary consecutive interior angles.

reviews.scope: Proving the triangle midsegment theorem via auxiliary parallelogram construction
reviews.reason: Parallelogram criteria are required when proving the midsegment theorem by doubling the segment to form a parallelogram, whereas alternative proofs avoid parallelograms.
reviews.counterexample: The triangle midsegment theorem can be proved directly using SAS triangle similarity from the 1:2 side ratios and shared vertex angle, or via coordinate geometry.

reviews.scope: Defining triangle midsegments and computing segment lengths using midpoints
reviews.reason: Defining a triangle midsegment as the segment joining two side midpoints and calculating related segment lengths directly require the concept and properties of segment midpoints.

reviews.scope: Understanding and proving rectangle angle, side, and diagonal properties
reviews.reason: A rectangle is defined as a special parallelogram and directly inherits opposite-side equality and diagonal bisection to establish and apply its own properties.

reviews.scope: Proving the right-triangle hypotenuse median theorem using rectangle diagonals
reviews.reason: The mastery criteria explicitly require proving the hypotenuse median theorem via a rectangle, which directly relies on a rectangle having equal and mutually bisecting diagonals.

reviews.scope: Identifying and constructing the median to the hypotenuse
reviews.reason: Understanding and applying the theorem about the median to a right triangle's hypotenuse requires knowing the definition of a triangle median as the vertex-to-midpoint segment.

reviews.scope: Formulating and proving the criteria for identifying a rectangle
reviews.reason: Rectangle identification criteria build directly on the definition of a rectangle and invert its right-angle and equal-diagonal properties established in the properties topic.

reviews.scope: Proving a quadrilateral is a rectangle via parallelogram-based criteria
reviews.reason: Both the definition-based and equal-diagonal criteria for a rectangle require first establishing that the figure is a parallelogram using parallelogram criteria.

reviews.scope: Deriving and applying the side and diagonal properties of rhombuses
reviews.reason: A rhombus is defined as a special parallelogram and relies on parallelogram properties, particularly mutually bisecting diagonals and equal opposite sides, to establish its own properties.

reviews.scope: Proving rhombus diagonals are perpendicular and bisect interior angles
reviews.reason: Isosceles triangle three-lines-in-one provides a concise proof that rhombus diagonals are perpendicular angle bisectors, but this property can also be proved via congruent triangles.
reviews.counterexample: Since opposite sides are equal and diagonals bisect each other, the four sub-triangles are congruent by SSS, directly proving perpendicularity and angle bisection without isosceles triangle theorems.

reviews.scope: Calculating rhombus side lengths and areas from diagonal lengths
reviews.reason: Because rhombus diagonals are perpendicular bisectors forming four right triangles, the Pythagorean theorem is the standard tool linking half-diagonals to the side length in metric problems.
reviews.counterexample: Rhombus side lengths can be found directly from perimeter or special 60-degree equilateral triangles, and area can be computed directly when both diagonal lengths are given.

reviews.scope: Formulating and proving the criteria for identifying a rhombus
reviews.reason: Rhombus identification criteria directly use the definition of a rhombus and invert its four-equal-sides and perpendicular-diagonals properties established in the properties topic.

reviews.scope: Proving a quadrilateral is a rhombus via parallelogram-based criteria
reviews.reason: Both the adjacent-side and perpendicular-diagonal criteria for a rhombus require first establishing that the quadrilateral is a parallelogram using parallelogram criteria.

reviews.scope: Proving the perpendicular-diagonal criterion for a rhombus
reviews.reason: When a parallelogram has perpendicular diagonals, one diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other, immediately yielding equal adjacent sides via the perpendicular bisector property.
reviews.counterexample: Equal adjacent sides can also be proved directly by SAS triangle congruence on the right triangles formed by the bisecting diagonals without citing the perpendicular bisector theorem.

reviews.scope: Proving a quadrilateral is a square and organizing quadrilateral hierarchy
reviews.reason: Because a square is both a rectangle and a rhombus, proving a quadrilateral is a square and establishing the four-quadrilateral inclusion hierarchy require rectangle criteria.

reviews.scope: Proving a quadrilateral is a square and organizing quadrilateral hierarchy
reviews.reason: Identifying a square as a rectangle with rhombus conditions or a rhombus with rectangle conditions and mapping quadrilateral inclusions directly require rhombus criteria.

reviews.scope: Using special quadrilateral properties in folding and moving-point problems
reviews.reason: Analyzing folding and moving-point configurations in rectangles, rhombuses, and squares requires applying the side, angle, and diagonal properties of these special quadrilaterals.

reviews.scope: Setting up Pythagorean equations in quadrilateral folding problems
reviews.reason: Finding segment lengths in quadrilateral folding and moving-point problems explicitly requires transferring equal segments under folding into a right triangle and applying the Pythagorean theorem to form equations.

reviews.scope: Identifying variables and constants in algebraic relationship examples
reviews.reason: Writing algebraic expressions helps symbolize quantitative relationships when illustrating variables and constants, though the concept itself only requires distinguishing changing quantities from fixed ones.
reviews.counterexample: Variables and constants can be identified directly from verbal descriptions, data tables, or real-life processes without constructing algebraic expressions.

reviews.scope: Defining functions as correspondences between two variables
reviews.reason: The definition of a function as a single-valued dependence between two changing quantities and the identification of independent and dependent variables directly require the concept of variables.

reviews.scope: Understanding directional pairing between independent and dependent variable values
reviews.reason: Ordered pairs provide a helpful prior analogy for pairing each input value with its corresponding output value in a fixed order where roles are not interchangeable.
reviews.counterexample: A function can be understood directly as a process where each value of one changing quantity uniquely determines another, without referencing positional ordered pairs.

reviews.scope: Understanding and finding the domain of a function's independent variable
reviews.reason: Determining the permissible values of a function's independent variable requires first understanding what a function and its independent variable are.

reviews.scope: Determining the domain of functions containing algebraic fractions
reviews.reason: Finding the domain of rational function expressions directly requires the condition that an algebraic fraction is defined only when its denominator is nonzero.

reviews.scope: Determining the domain of functions containing square root expressions
reviews.reason: Finding the domain of function formulas containing square roots directly requires knowing that a square root expression is defined only when its radicand is nonnegative.

reviews.scope: Defining and finding function values and corresponding inputs
reviews.reason: Understanding a function value as the unique output corresponding to a given input and reversing the correspondence directly require the concept of a function.

reviews.scope: Computing function values by substituting input values into formulas
reviews.reason: Calculating the function value for a given input from an analytical formula directly requires substituting numbers into an algebraic expression and following the order of operations.

reviews.scope: Tabulating input-output pairs to plot graphs and reading function values
reviews.reason: Both constructing a table of coordinates to plot a function graph and reading output values for given inputs from a graph require the concept and calculation of function values.

reviews.scope: Plotting coordinate pairs and reading values on a function graph
reviews.reason: Drawing a function graph by plotting input-output pairs and reading values from the curve require constructing a Cartesian coordinate plane and mapping between points and coordinates.

reviews.scope: Interpreting increasing and decreasing trends from a function graph
reviews.reason: Prior experience reading how quantities rise or fall over time in trend charts provides helpful visual intuition for describing change trends on a function graph.
reviews.counterexample: Students can read function values and change trends directly from Cartesian coordinates and point-by-point comparisons without prior study of statistical trend charts.

reviews.scope: Comparing function representations and converting between graphs, tables, and formulas
reviews.reason: Because a graph is one of the three core function representations, comparing the three forms and converting among them directly require understanding and constructing function graphs.

reviews.scope: Translating real-world data into function formulas and analyzing change
reviews.reason: Understanding the three function representations helps students extract formulas from tables or graphs and analyze change, though writing formulas and domains from word problems does not require all three representations.
reviews.counterexample: A student can write a function formula and determine its practical domain directly from verbal quantitative relationships using algebraic expressions and domain constraints without comparing tables or graphs.

reviews.scope: Formulating analytical expressions for real-world patterns of change
reviews.reason: Inducing an algebraic expression for the nth term of a sequence builds helpful pattern-generalization skills for writing function formulas that describe real-world quantitative changes.
reviews.counterexample: Many real-world function formulas follow directly from standard rate, geometry, or pricing relationships without inductive sequence pattern finding.

reviews.scope: Motivating the algebraic definition y = kx of direct proportionality functions
reviews.reason: Elementary direct proportion where two positive quantities maintain a constant ratio provides helpful conceptual motivation for y = kx, though the function is defined and analyzed algebraically across all real numbers.
reviews.counterexample: A student can identify y = kx (k != 0), solve for k by substitution, and graph the line through the origin directly from function and coordinate definitions.

reviews.scope: Connecting the formula y = kx with its tabular values and line graph
reviews.reason: Converting among formulas, tables, and graphs prepares students to link y = kx with its straight-line graph, though comparing the pros and cons of the three representations is not required.
reviews.counterexample: A student who understands function formulas and how to plot function graphs can identify y = kx, solve for k, and draw its graph without studying the comparative merits of all three representation types.

reviews.scope: Understanding direct proportionality functions as the b = 0 special case
reviews.reason: The concept scope explicitly requires recognizing direct proportionality functions y = kx as the b = 0 special case of linear functions y = kx + b.

reviews.scope: Graphing linear functions y = kx + b and finding their axis intercepts
reviews.reason: Graphing a linear function and finding its intercepts with the coordinate axes require understanding the analytical form y = kx + b (k != 0) of a linear function.

reviews.scope: Finding the x-axis and y-axis intercepts of a linear function
reviews.reason: Finding the intersection points of y = kx + b with the coordinate axes requires knowing that points on the x-axis have ordinate 0 and points on the y-axis have abscissa 0.

reviews.scope: Determining line tilt, y-intercept, and quadrants passed through from k and b
reviews.reason: Analyzing how k and b govern the line's inclination, y-axis intercept, and quadrant locations directly builds on graphing linear functions as straight lines and finding their axis intercepts.

reviews.scope: Translating the straight-line graph of a linear function vertically
reviews.reason: Understanding and deriving the equation of a translated linear function graph require knowing that y = kx + b represents a line in the coordinate plane and how points lie on it.

reviews.scope: Deriving the analytical formula of a translated linear function graph
reviews.reason: Showing that shifting the line y = kx + b up or down by m units produces y = kx + b +- m directly relies on how point coordinates change under vertical translations.

reviews.scope: Setting up the general linear function form y = kx + b
reviews.reason: Applying the method of undetermined coefficients begins by assuming the general analytical form y = kx + b (k != 0), which directly requires the concept of a linear function.

reviews.scope: Solving the two-variable linear system for k and b
reviews.reason: Substitution elimination is one algebraic method for solving the system of equations in k and b obtained by plugging two points into y = kx + b.
reviews.counterexample: Because the constant term b has coefficient 1 in both equations, subtracting one equation from the other via addition-subtraction elimination solves for k and b directly without substitution.

reviews.scope: Solving the two-variable linear system for k and b
reviews.reason: Addition-subtraction elimination is one specific method for eliminating b from the two-equation system formed by substituting two coordinate pairs into y = kx + b.
reviews.counterexample: The system for k and b can alternatively be solved by expressing b in terms of k from one equation and using substitution elimination.

reviews.scope: Relating solutions of kx + b = 0 to x-intercepts of y = kx + b
reviews.reason: Connecting a one-variable linear equation to a linear function relies on understanding the straight-line graph of y = kx + b and its intersection with the x-axis.

reviews.scope: Connecting algebraic solutions of kx + b = 0 with graphical x-intercepts
reviews.reason: Explaining how solving kx + b = 0 corresponds to finding where the function y = kx + b takes value 0 requires knowing how to solve one-variable linear equations.

reviews.scope: Reading inequality solution sets from the graph of y = kx + b
reviews.reason: Determining the x-values where y = kx + b lies above or below the x-axis directly requires understanding the straight-line graph of a linear function and its axis intercepts.

reviews.scope: Connecting algebraic solution sets of kx + b > 0 with linear graphs
reviews.reason: Linking one-variable linear inequalities to linear function graphs and expressing the corresponding x-intervals as inequality solution sets require understanding linear inequalities and their solutions.

reviews.scope: Interpreting the intersection of two linear function graphs as a common solution
reviews.reason: Relating a two-variable linear system to the intersection point of two lines requires knowing how to graph linear functions and interpret coordinates of points on those lines.

reviews.scope: Identifying line intersection coordinates as the solution of a two-variable linear system
reviews.reason: Explaining why the intersection point of two lines gives the solution of the corresponding linear system requires understanding what a two-variable linear system and its common solution mean.

reviews.scope: Finding the intersection point of two lines by solving their linear system
reviews.reason: Substitution elimination is one specific algebraic method for solving the system of two linear function equations to find their intersection coordinates.
reviews.counterexample: The system of two linear equations can also be solved by subtracting the equations via addition-subtraction elimination to eliminate y directly.
